correctness.rationale: This pass applies to the complete corrected RESULT.md, not an unrestricted reading of the frozen relaxation paragraph. The frozen paragraph sets theta but does not reinstate q=1/2 after discussing other orientations, whereas its proof uses lambda tending to zero and the balanced norm coefficient. The relaxation assertion as stated for arbitrary fixed q fails: set alpha=1, beta=3, v=e1 and omega=0 in the two stages. They give H=diag(0,-1/2) for every t, so the first norm divided by t tends to 0 rather than 1/4 and the radius stays 1/2 rather than tending to 0. The repair explicitly fixes the balanced overlap in the relaxation finding and proof; the exact orientation formulas remain valid for all q. Subtracting the true fixed point and eliminating the half step yields G=theta I+(1-theta)C^{-1}DB with D=d e2 e2^T. Its rank-one trace and the product of its generating vector norms give the orientation laws. Their dependence on q(1-q) proves the strict opposite extrema in q, not uniqueness of a signed vector v. At balance, H^k=lambda^(k-1)H gives the unrelaxed stiff limits, and direct substitution gives the angular-window result. The repaired relaxed proof uses the two eigenvalues and the binomial coefficient p_k(lambda), with lambda tending to zero specifically at balance. The reverse-triangle bound and the uniform k r^(k-1) tail for fixed theta<1 justify the limit of the supremum, including theta=0. The ratio theta(k+1)/k certifies the leading index and integer ties. Independently reconstructing the two stage solves confirmed the examples: at alpha=1,beta=3,q=1/2,t=1000, ||H||/t≈0.250000375 and ||H²||≈0.125000125; at theta=3/4 the leading coefficient is 27/256, tied at k=3,4, not at finite t. Direct replay inputs are the two displayed stages with these values, or alpha=1,beta=3,v=e1,omega=0 for the scope counterexample. The frozen `verify.py` was inspected, not run. The repaired file retains and proves the fixed-t transformed contraction; no claim extends to joint theta approaching one or to higher-dimensional systems.
